title: Materials
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Materials.

concepts.def: Long chains of repeating monomer units.
Mixtures of a metal with other elements, usually harder than the pure metal.
Hard, brittle, insulating materials such as clay and glass.
Two materials combined for improved properties (e.g. fibreglass).
Strength, hardness, conductivity chosen to suit a use.
Very small particles with a high surface area and special properties.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Materials — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Materials brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Materials.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why are alloys usually harder than pure metals?
options: Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily
Alloys contain stronger covalent bonds throughout
Alloy atoms are all identical in size
Alloys have no free electrons

mcqs.q: Steel is an alloy of iron and:
options: Carbon
Aluminium
Copper
Zinc
Many ethene monomers joining into long chains
Ethene molecules dissolving in each other
Cracking long hydrocarbon chains
Burning ethene in limited oxygen

mcqs.q: Metals conduct electricity because they have:
options: Delocalised electrons that are free to move
Free-moving protons
Vibrating neutrons
Ions free to move in the solid
Alloys are pure elements that have simply been melted.
No — an alloy is a mixture; its components are not chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and the proportions can be varied.
Alloys are compounds because the metals are chemically joined together.
Pure metals are harder because their atoms are heavier than alloy atoms.

mcqs.q: Are pure metals harder than alloys?
options: Pure metals are harder because they have no impurities to weaken them.
Alloys are pure elements that have simply been melted.
Usually softer — the identical atoms in a pure metal form regular layers that slide over each other easily; alloying disrupts these layers.
Pure metals are harder because their atoms are heavier than alloy atoms.

mcqs.q: Do plastics rot away quickly in landfill?
options: Buried plastics decompose within a few years like food waste does.
No — most plastics are non-biodegradable; microorganisms cannot break them down, so they persist for very many years.
Alloys are pure elements that have simply been melted.
Plastics slowly evaporate until they disappear completely.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Choosing materials”?
options: An alloy of iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon; it is harder and stronger than pure iron.
Metals conduct electricity and heat and can be shaped because delocalised electrons move between layers of positive ions.
Plastics are typically flexible, electrically insulating and low-density, but most are not biodegradable, creating disposal problems.
Materials are selected for a job by matching properties such as strength, density, conductivity, flexibility and cost to the use.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Metallic properties”?
options: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements; the different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, making alloys harder than pure metals.
Metals conduct electricity and heat and can be shaped because delocalised electrons move between layers of positive ions.
Materials are selected for a job by matching properties such as strength, density, conductivity, flexibility and cost to the use.
An alloy of iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon; it is harder and stronger than pure iron.

A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements; the different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, making alloys harder than pure metals.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Properties of plastics”?
options: Metals conduct electricity and heat and can be shaped because delocalised electrons move between layers of positive ions.
Materials are selected for a job by matching properties such as strength, density, conductivity, flexibility and cost to the use.
Plastics are typically flexible, electrically insulating and low-density, but most are not biodegradable, creating disposal problems.
A very long-chain molecule made by joining many small monomer units together, as in poly(ethene) made from ethene.
